list.listitem: Cerumen is a waxy substance produced by glands in the outer part of the ear canal, removed naturally by epithelial migration. It helps protect the ear from dust, dirt, infection, and water. A

Routine cerumen removal is unnecessary if the ears can be examined efficiently and are asymptomatic. In children and cognitively-impaired persons who cannot express symptoms, evaluate and treat as needed. C
Perform otoscopy on patients complaining of ear discomfort or decreased hearing and routinely in persons using hearing aids even if they are asymptomatic. C
Treat cerumen impaction with one or more of the following: cerumenolytic agents, irrigation, manual removal with instruments, or combination; if failed, refer to a clinician who can treat. B

Among the cerumenolytics available, minimal evidence exists that one is better. Using any cerumenolytic appears to be better than no treatment. Saline alone is as effective as commonly used cerumenolytics for removing impacted cerumen. B ,
Removal may be easier with curettage under direct otoscopic visualization. C Document the condition of the tympanic membrane following cerumen removal. C

Self-help measures such as washing the outer ear with soap and water and regular instillation of cerumenolytic agents like emollient oil, triethanolamine, carbamide peroxide, and docusate sodium may decrease the recurrence of cerumen impaction. B

background.definition: Cerumen, or earwax, is a waxy substance that is part of a natural process that cleans, protects, and lubricates the external auditory canal. Cerumen impaction occurs when cerumen or earwax builds up and blocks the ear canal, making it difficult to examine the ear canal, eardrum, and/or audio-vestibular system. Evaluation by otoscope should be conducted if symptomatic with hearing loss, itching, discomfort, ringing in the ears, discharge, odor, ear pain, feeling of fullness in the ear, cough or imbalance to ensure proper treatment and prevent any further complications.

list.listitem: The prevalence of cerumen impaction is 6% in the general population, with increased prevalence among those with cognitive impairment and elderly patients (35%).

About 4% of the general population (2.3 million people in UK and 12 million in US) consults primary care for cerumen problems, 2% to 6% suffer from cerumen impaction at any given time with 4 million ears syringed annually.

Excessive or impacted cerumen may be present in 1 in 10 children, 1 in 20 adults and more than 1 in 3 elderly indivuduals. Is is common among those with developmental and pathological disorders of ear canal (e.g., recurrent otitis externa; keratosis obturans; prior radiation therapy affecting the ear; exostoses or osteoma; neoplasms of the ear canal; previous tympanoplasty/ myringoplasty, canal wall down mastoidectomy, or other surgery affecting the ear canal).

Among kindergarten-aged children in China assessed in 2005, 2006, and 2012, prevalence of cerumen impaction was 10% to 17.2%. Impaction was more commonly observed in children with dry vs. wet cerumen (22% vs. 5%).
In a Finnish screening study of 61 patients with schizophrenia, cerumen impaction was found in 12 (19.7%).

In United States, cerumen impaction accounts for 12 million patient visits and 8 million cerumen removal procedures. In 2012, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services reimbursed $46.8 million for 1.3 million cerumen dis-impactions (mean, $35.38 per procedure); one third were performed in family practices.

Cerumen impaction has significant impact on hearing ability and cognitive function in the elderly. Among 55 Japanese patients, both hearing and Mini Mental State Examination score improved significantly after cerumen removal in patients whose impaction was in the better hearing ear than for patients who did not have cerumen impaction or had it in the worse hearing ear.

A small cross-sectional study detected SARS-Co V2 virus in cerumen samples of both symptomatic and asymptomatic patients; there was no conclusion regarding cerumen as a potential source of spread. On the contrary, investigators in another small prospective study of SARS-CoV-2 patients did not detect any SARS-CoV-2 virus in cerumen samples.
Cerumen or earwax, is a natural part of the process that cleans, protects, and lubricates the external auditory canal. Impaction occurs when cerumen accumulates in the external auditory canal.
Risk factors are poorly studied but may include age, ethnic background, stenosed ear canal, environment, hearing aid use and cognitive impairment.
Use of cotton swabs, ear candling, oil drops or sprays and oral jet irrigators for self-cleaning are controversial causes.

Natural process: Cerumen, a natural hydrophobic , waxy substance formed from the glandular secretions of the outer two thirds of the ear canal mixed with desquamated epithelium protects, cleans and lubricates the external auditory canal. Cerumen is usually cleared by a self-cleaning mechanism, with migration of the canal’s epithelial lining, aided by jaw movement

Phenotype concerns: Based on genetic phenotype, cerumen can be divided into dry (Asian and Native American) or wet (African and European decent), but it is unclear if phenotypic variation leads to impaction.
Production concerns: Symptomatic occlusion from overproduction of cerumen which exceeds natural clearance. Recurrent impaction is possible in idiopathic cerumen overproduction.

Clearance concerns: Inadequate cerumen clearance is secondary to improper epithelial migration of the ear canal. Factors such as aging can slow down cerumen migration (dry cerumen, atrophy of cerumen glands, coarse hair). Conditions like chronic otitis media can alter the epithelium's migratory pattern, complicating the ear's self-cleaning mechanism. Failure of standard cerumen clearance mechanisms can lead to occlusion of the external auditory canal.

Mechanical concerns: Other contributing factors are narrow ear canals, exposure to noisy surroundings, regular use of cotton-tipped swabs, dry cerumen (found in older adults as ceruminous glands atrophy), and foreign objects placed in the ear (e.g., hearing aids and ear plugs).

There are no United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommendations that directly address screening for cerumen impaction. The USPSTF also found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for hearing loss in asymptomatic adults aged 50 years or older. C

Clinicians should educate and counsel patients with recurrent cerumen impaction and those who are susceptible (children, older adults, people using hearing aids, exposure to noise pollution or who have cognitive impairment) on safe and effective preventive measures: Regular hygiene - gentle cleaning with a damp cloth around the outer ear. Avoid excessive cleaning to avoid harm such as scrapes or unintended impaction caused by manipulation and allow earwax to naturally move out. Regular check-ups - encourage routine ear examinations. C

Self-help measures such as washing the outer ear with soap and water and regular instillation of cerumenolytic agents like emollient oil, triethanolamine, carbamide peroxide, and docusate sodium may decrease the recurrence of cerumen impaction. C

In one RCT, ear self-irrigation with a bulb syringe following an episode of symptomatic cerumen impaction was more effective than an ear drop instilled prior to a nurse visit (control group) on return visits for episodes of cerumen (60% vs. 73% for controls; number needed to treat = 8; 95% CI, 4-143). B
Educate proper care of hearing aids with Tips to Clean and Keep the Ear Canal Unobstructed.

Perform otoscopy on patients complaining of ear discomfort or decreased hearing and at least once every six months for patients wearing hearing aids, children and cognitively-impaired persons. B No intervention is needed if asymptomatic. Intervention is recommended for special populations (e.g., children and cognitively-imparired persons) who cannot express symptoms. C
Diagnose cerumen impaction when an accumulation of cerumen is visualized by otoscopy and associated with symptoms, and/or prevents assessment of the ear. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Purulent drainage, inflammation of the external auditory canal
Visible abnormalities of the tympanic membrane (TM), decreased mobility of the TM with pneumatic otoscopy

Differential.Differential_Name: Foreign body occlusion of the external auditory canal

Differential.Differential_Features: Diagnostic findings on Rinne and Weber testing and audiometry

list.listitem: Initial symptoms of cerumen impaction may include decreased hearing or hearing loss, tinnitus, itching, ear pain, ear discharge, discomfort, or sensation of ear fullness.
Otoscopic evaluation is recommended to confirm retention of cerumen in the external auditory canal.

The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation recommend that, for optimal care and safe outcomes in patients with cerumen impaction, clinicians should screen for factors that may modify management such as: anticoagulant therapy, immunocompromised state, diabetes mellitus, prior radiation therapy to the head and neck, ear canal stenosis, exostoses, and nonintact tympanic membrane.
C

Recommend evaluation by otoscope if symptomatic with hearing loss, itching, discomfort, ringing in the ears, discharge, odor, ear pain, feeling of fullness in the ear, cough, or imbalance to ensure proper treatment and prevent any further complications.
Audiometry may help quantify hearing loss and verify response to treatment.
Cerumen in asymptomatic patients: watchful waiting is reasonable as self-resolution is noted in up to one-third of episodes B .
Cerumen in symptomatic patients: Treatment aims to improve symptoms, view tympanic membranes, and allow audiometric evaluations for diagnostic purposes. C

Otoscopy should be performed on patients with symptoms suggestive of cerumen impaction, those who cannot express symptoms like children and cognitively-impaired persons, and in patients using hearing aids. B

In a study on developmentally-delayed individuals at a residential facility who had 50% to 80% of their external ear canal blocked by cerumen without any conductive hearing loss, only 3% progressed to impaction with associated hearing loss; 44% had no cerumen and 53% had the same amount but no conductive hearing loss at one-year follow up.

Before cerumen removal, rule out contraindications like nonintact tympanic membrane, exostosis, anatomical variations of the ear canal, diabetes mellitus, anticoagulation use, immunocompromised or prior local radiation to avoid risk of trauma, infection, or hemorrhage.
Among available cerumenolytics, there is no evidence that one is better than another. Saline ear drops may be as effective as commonly used cerumenolytics for the removal of impacted cerumen. B ,
Manual cerumen removal may be easier with curettage under direct otoscopic visualization, and wet irrigation was better than dry irrigation. C
Ear candling, olive oil/spray, foreign objects like cotton-tipped swabs, pens/pen tops, paper clips are not recommended due to safety concerns and lack of proven efficacy. B
The condition of the tympanic membrane should be documented following cerumen removal. B

Agents used to break down cerumen are called cerumenolytics. Cerumenolytics work by hydrating the keratin cells of desquamated stratum corneum and subsequently inducing keratolysis, with disintegration of wax. The use of a cerumenolytic will improve success of subsequent irrigation and is also associated with significantly less reported pain and vertigo.

Commonly used cerumenolytics include water-based agents (e.g. acetic acid, triethanolamine, docusate sodium, hydrogen peroxide, sodium bicarbonate, sterile saline solution), oil-based agents (e.g. almond oil, Arachis oil, olive oil, mineral oil and liquid petrolatum), or non-oil /non-water based agents (e.g. audax and carbamide peroxide). Comparative efficacy is unclear, and one may be no better than another.

Authors of a systematic review concluded that cerumol, sodium bicarbonate, olive oil and water were all better than no treatment; that triethanolamine polypeptide was better than olive oil; that nurses were better than patients at irrigating; and that wet irrigation was better than dry irrigation.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 10 studies of poor quality, with 623 patients found that cerumenolytic drops seemed to be better than no drops, with no clear evidence favoring one cerumenolytic over another.

In a RCT of 1243 children aged 5 to 16 years who had cerumen plugs occluding at least 90% of the canal, children were randomized to one of 5 different solutions and instructed to use 10 drops 3 times daily with attempts at cerumen aspiration via micro-suction completed at 3, 6 and 10 days. At day 3, the solution containing a mixture of glycerin 10 cc + 3% hydrogen peroxide 10 cc + 10% sodium bicarbonate 10 cc + distilled water 10 cc resulted in significantly less reported pain and more children who had total tympanic membrane (TM) visualization compared to the other groups (73.5% vs. 44.3%-62.3%). However, by day 6, all children had visualized TMs.
Avoid use of cerumenolytics if there is non-intact tympanic membrane, active dermatitis, or infection of the ear canal.

A recent RCT by Asgari et al., in which carbamide peroxide and phenol glycerin were compared, suggested that carbamide peroxide was superior treatment for patients with external ear canal obstruction caused by cerumen impaction because it was more effective in cerumen degradation and had no reported side effects.

Manual cerumen removal with use of a curettage, metal/plastic loop or spoon under direct otoscopic visualization may be easier and quicker than irrigation and is the preferred technique for patients with abnormal ear canal anatomy, a history of ear surgery, systemic illnesses that increase the risk of infection, or a nonintact tympanic membrane. Common risks following manual removal are tympanic membrane perforation, ear canal trauma, vertigo and otalgia.

Irrigation of the external auditory canal is a commonly performed office procedure, used by 95% of general practioners. A variety of irrigation devices are commercially available. Wet irrigation was better than dry irrigation.
One in 3 patients with cerumen impaction will experience a mean hearing improvement of 5 dB with irrigation.

An estimated 1 in 1000 patients experience complications following syringing for cerumen impaction including tinnitus, tympanic membrane perforation, damage to the external auditory canal, pain, vertigo, incomplete removal, bleeding, and otitis externa.
Syringing can predispose to otitis media and otitis externa, and retention of water behind incompletely removed cerumen increases this risk.

Aural micro-suction, usually performed by oan tolaryngologistsunder direct vision with a binocular operating microscope, is another technique for cerumen removal. The procedure was 91% successful for viewing the tympanic membrane based on a survey of 159 patients. On a scale of 1 to 10, patients reported only minimal pain (2.3 points), noise discomfort (3.0 points), or vertigo (2.0 points).The procedure decreases exposure of the ear to moisture and is associated with a lower frequency of infections.
Following removal of cerumen reacidification of the ear canal with 2% acetic acid can help prevent bacterial colonization that can lead to otitis externa.
Contraindications to irrigation are previous ear surgery, perforated tympanic membrane, history of otitis externa, ear canal abnormalities, and cerumen impaction in the only or better hearing ear.

Ear candling and oil (olive oil, natural oil, baby oil, mineral oils or glycerin) are popular alternative therapy for cerumen impaction but recommended against due to associated risks. Not recommended if ear drum rupture or active ear infection is suspected. Nearly one fifth of surveyed otolaryngologists reported injuries associated with candle use. C

Self-help measures, such as washing the outer ear with soap and water and regular instillation of cerumenolytic agents like emollient oil, triethanolamine, carbamide peroxide, and docusate sodium may decrease the recurrence of cerumen impaction. B
Self-irrigation of ears with a bulb syringe also appears to reduce return visits for episodes of cerumen.
If full or partial symptoms persist despite resolution of the cerumen impaction, the clinician should evaluate the patient for alternative diagnoses.

Clinicians should consider referral to clinicians who have specialized equipment and training to clean and evaluate ear canals and tympanic membranes for patients with failure to remove cerumen after multiple attempts of syringing, chronic cerumen impaction, abnormal tissue in the ear canal, visibly perforated tympanic membrane, and if significant pain, bleeding or vertigo develops.

Most cases of cerumen impaction are not dangerous and can be managed effectively. Symptoms such as ear fullness, hearing loss, and discomfort usually improve with treatment. Removal of occlusive cerumen improves hearing for 1 in 3 patients by a mean of 5 dB. B
Complications of cerumen removal are rare, but can occur during or after removal. These include:
Ear Canal Injury: During the removal process, there is a risk of injuring the delicate tissues lining the ear canals.
Infection: Using unsterilized instruments or any breakage in the skin can serve as potential sources of infection.
Vertigo and Dizziness: Disturbance of the inner ear canal can cause sensations of imbalance and vertigo.
Tympanic Membrane Rupture: Rarely, excessive force during removal may cause a perforated eardrum.
Caloric Stimulation Symptoms: Cold irrigation water can induce symptoms like vertigo, bradycardia, and nausea.
Necrotizing External Otitis: Particularly in patients with diabetes, this severe infection can occur.
Regular ear hygiene and preventive measures can help maintain ear health.

Cerumen is a naturally occurring substance formed from the glandular secretions of the outer two thirds of the ear canal mixed with desquamated epithelium that protects, cleans and lubricates the external auditory canal.
Cerumen is usually cleared by self-cleaning mechanism and up to one-third of cases of cerumen impaction will clear within five days without treatment.
